title: Veteran property tax exemptions, by disability and circumstance
summary: Massachusetts has a ladder of Veteran exemptions rather than one. Each gives you the greater of a cut in assessed valuation or a flat cut in the tax itself, starting at $400 off your bill with a 10 percent rating and rising with disability.
amount: From $2,000 of valuation or $400 of tax at a 10 percent rating, up to $10,000 of valuation or $1,500 of tax, with full exemption in some cases
eligibility: You are a legal resident of Massachusetts
And you were domiciled in Massachusetts for at least six months before entering service, or have been a resident for two consecutive years before filing
A city or town may lower that residency requirement to one year before filing
Clause 22, the base: a service-connected disability rating of 10 percent or more gives $2,000 of valuation or $400 of tax

Clause 22A: loss of use of one foot at or above the ankle or one hand at or above the wrist, a statutory award for loss of one eye, the Medal of Honor, Distinguished Service Cross, Navy Cross or Air Force Cross, or prisoner of war status, gives $4,000 or $750
Clause 22B: loss of both feet, both hands, one foot and one hand, or sight of both eyes, gives $8,000 or $1,250
Clause 22C: permanent and total disability in line of duty with assistance acquiring specially adapted housing gives $10,000 or $1,500
Clause 22E: a 100 percent VA disability rating from service-connected disabilities gives $6,000 or $1,000
Clause 22F: paraplegia, or a 100 percent rating for service-connected blindness, covers the domicile with no dollar figure stated
details: Read the amounts carefully. Each clause says whichever would result in an abatement of the greater amount of actual taxes due, so you get the better of a reduction in assessed valuation or a flat reduction in the tax. The first figure is valuation, the second is tax. For most homes the flat tax figure is the one that bites.
Qualifying factors such as age and ownership are determined as of 1 July each year.

You cannot stack these. A person receiving an exemption under clauses 22 through 22G cannot also take another Section 5 exemption on the same property, with narrow exceptions for clauses Eighteenth and Forty-fifth.

Two clauses are worth asking your town about, because they can increase everything above. Clause 22I, where accepted by the city or town and certified by the commissioner of revenue, increases the abatement annually by the rise in the cost of living under CPI. Clause 22J, also on local acceptance, allows an additional exemption of up to 100 percent of what you already qualify for, set by the local legislative body and applied uniformly.
Because 22I and 22J depend on local acceptance, two Veterans with identical ratings in neighbouring towns can receive very different amounts. Ask your assessor which clauses your town has accepted.
Clause 22G extends clauses 22 through 22F to property held by a trustee, conservator or other fiduciary for your benefit, but only where the city or town has accepted it.
The base clause also covers Spanish American War service, Purple Heart recipients with no proof of disability needed, spouses and surviving spouses, and parents of those who died in service.
agency: Local boards of assessors, with cost shared between the municipality and the Commonwealth
statuteRef: M.G.L. c. 59, s. 5, clauses Twenty-second through Twenty-second J

title: Full property tax exemption for surviving spouses and parents
summary: Massachusetts exempts the entire taxable valuation of the home for a surviving spouse of a service member who died from service, and for surviving parents or guardians where the town has accepted that clause.
amount: The full taxable valuation, with no dollar cap
eligibility: Clause 22D, surviving spouse: the service member died from a service-connected injury or illness documented by the VA or a branch of the armed forces, or is missing in action with a presumptive finding of death
For clause 22D the surviving spouse must have been domiciled in Massachusetts for the two consecutive years before filing, or the service member domiciled here at least six months before service
Clause 22H, surviving parent or guardian: the same death or missing in action condition applies
For clause 22H the parent or guardian must have been domiciled in Massachusetts for the five consecutive years immediately before filing
Clause 22H applies only where the city or town has accepted it
details: These are full exemptions of the taxable valuation, not the capped amounts that apply to the disability clauses, so they are worth far more.
Clause 22D took effect for tax years beginning on or after 1 January 2017 and is funded by the Commonwealth rather than the municipality.

Clause 22H took effect for tax years beginning on or after 1 January 2019 and remains available until the parent or guardian dies. Because it needs local acceptance, check with your assessor whether your town has adopted it.
Note the residency difference. A surviving spouse needs two consecutive years of Massachusetts domicile before filing, while a surviving parent or guardian needs five.
The annual cost of living increase in clause 22I and the local additional exemption in clause 22J are listed for the disability clauses rather than for 22D, 22G or 22H.
agency: Local boards of assessors, with clause 22D funded by the Commonwealth
statuteRef: M.G.L. c. 59, s. 5, clauses Twenty-second D and Twenty-second H

title: Military retirement pay is not taxed
summary: Massachusetts excludes US government retirement pay for retired members of the uniformed services from state gross income, with no cap and no age test. Survivor benefits are covered too.
amount: Full exclusion, with no dollar cap
eligibility: The income is received from the United States government as retirement pay for a retired member of the uniformed services, as defined in 10 U.S.C. 1072
Survivorship benefits under 10 U.S.C. 1431 to 1460 are also excluded
The exclusion applies regardless of whether the retiree contributed to the retirement system
details: No condition on age, amount, residency or length of service appears in this provision.

This covers retirement pay. Active duty pay is not covered by this subparagraph, so treat that as a separate question. There is a related rule at Section 5A(c) treating active duty pay at Massachusetts posts as out of state income for nonresidents.
The same subparagraph also covers contributory state and federal pensions, so it is a broad provision rather than a Veteran-specific one.
